paragraphs: To keep the people from seeing too clearly what this arrangement would lead to, Servius tried to give it a military look. In the second class he placed two centuries of armorers, and in the fourth two of makers of weapons. In every class except the last he separated young and old, that is, those obliged to bear arms from those whose age legally exempted them. This distinction, more than that of wealth, made it necessary to repeat the census, or counting, often. Finally, he ordered the assembly to be held in the Campus Martius, and everyone of an age to serve to come there armed.

He did not make this division of young and old in the last class as well because the common people who composed it were not granted the right to bear arms for their country. A man had to own a hearth to acquire the right to defend it. Of all the troops of beggars who today lend luster to the armies of kings, there is perhaps not one who would not have been driven with scorn out of a Roman cohort, in the days when soldiers were the defenders of liberty.

In this last class, however, _proletarians_ were distinguished from _capite censi._ The former, not quite reduced to nothing, at least supplied the State with citizens, and sometimes, when the need was pressing, even with soldiers. Those who had nothing at all and could only be counted by heads were regarded as worth nothing whatever, and Marius was the first to stoop to enlisting them.

I will not decide here whether this third arrangement was good or bad in itself. I think I can say that it was workable only because of the simple morals, the lack of self-interest, the love of farming and the scorn for trade and for the love of gain that marked the early Romans. Where is the modern people among whom devouring greed, restlessness, intrigue, constant moving about and endless swings of fortune could let such a system last twenty years without turning the State upside down? We should also note that morality and the censorship, being stronger than this institution, corrected its defects at Rome, and that a rich man found himself demoted to the class of the poor for making too much display of his wealth.

From all this it is easy to see why only five classes are almost always mentioned, though there were really six. The sixth supplied neither soldiers to the army nor votes in the Campus Martius,[1] and had almost no function in the State, so it was seldom thought to count for anything.

These were the various ways the Roman people was divided. Now let us see what effect they had on the assemblies. When lawfully summoned, these assemblies were called _comitia_. They were usually held in the public square at Rome or in the Campus Martius, and were named _Comitia Curiata, Comitia Centuriata_, and _Comitia Tributa_ according to the form in which they were convened. The _Comitia Curiata_ were founded by Romulus, the _Centuriata_ by Servius, and the _Tributa_ by the tribunes of the people. No law was approved and no magistrate elected except in the comitia. Since every citizen was enrolled in a _curia_, a century or a tribe, it follows that no citizen was excluded from voting, and that the Roman people was truly sovereign both _de jure_ and _de facto_.

For the comitia to be lawfully assembled, and for their acts to have the force of law, three conditions were needed. First, the body or magistrate convening them had to have the necessary authority. Second, the assembly had to meet on a day the law allowed. Third, the auguries had to be favorable.

The reason for the first rule needs no explaining. The second is a matter of policy. For example, the comitia could not be held on festivals or market days, when country people came to Rome on business and had no time to spend the day in the public square. Through the third, the senate held the proud, restless people in check and properly restrained the ardor of seditious tribunes, who nonetheless found more than one way around this obstacle.

Laws and the election of rulers were not the only questions put to the judgment of the comitia. The Roman people had taken on the most important functions of government, so it may be said that the fate of Europe was decided in its assemblies. The variety of their business gave rise to the various forms the assemblies took, depending on the matters they had to decide.

To judge these various forms, it is enough to compare them. When Romulus set up the _curiæ_, he meant the people to check the senate and the senate to check the people, while he kept his own ascendancy over both. So through this assembly he gave the people all the authority of numbers, to balance the power and riches he left to the patricians. But in keeping with the spirit of monarchy, he still left the patricians a greater advantage, in the influence their clients had on the majority of votes. This excellent institution of patron and client was a masterpiece of statesmanship and humanity. Without it the patriciate, which flatly contradicted the republican spirit, could not have survived. Rome alone has the honor of having given the world this great example, which never led to any abuse and yet has never been followed.
The assemblies by _curiæ_ lasted under the kings until Servius, and the reign of the later Tarquin was not regarded as legitimate. So royal laws were generally called _leges curiatæ_.

Under the Republic, the _curiæ_ were still confined to the four urban tribes and included only the populace of Rome. They suited neither the senate, which led the patricians, nor the tribunes, who, though plebeians, headed the well-to-do citizens. So they fell into disrepute, and sank so low that thirty lictors would gather and do what the _Comitia Curiata_ should have done.

The division by centuries was so favorable to the aristocracy that at first it is hard to see how the senate ever failed to win in the comitia that bore their name, the ones that elected the consuls, the censors and the other curule magistrates. Of the hundred and ninety-three centuries into which the six classes of the whole Roman people were divided, the first class held ninety-eight. Since voting went by centuries alone, this class by itself had a majority over all the rest. When all these centuries agreed, the remaining votes were not even taken. The decision of the smallest number passed for that of the multitude, and it may be said that in the _Comitia Centuriata_ decisions were settled far more by the depth of purses than by the number of votes.

But this extreme authority was softened in two ways. First, the tribunes as a rule, and always a great number of plebeians, belonged to the class of the rich, and so they balanced the influence of the patricians in the first class.

The second way was this. The centuries were not made to vote straight through in order, which would always have meant starting with the first. Instead the Romans always picked one by lot, and it voted alone. Then on another day all the centuries were summoned in order of rank, the same election was repeated, and as a rule confirmed. In this way the authority of example was taken away from rank and given to the lot, on a democratic principle.
